c.tagline: A small capital where volcanoes, ice, and aurora collide.

taxi.fareNote: Starting fare around ISK 700 (~$5) plus a per-km rate; cards accepted everywhere; no tipping expected.

emergency.note: Iceland uses a single nationwide emergency number, 112, for police, medical, and fire; English-speaking operators are available and there is also a 112 Iceland safety-check app for travelers.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

avoid.reason: The Laugavegur bar strip gets rowdy with drunken crowds late on weekend nights; otherwise the city is exceptionally safe.

hood_desc: The historic downtown core packed with restaurants, bars, shops and Hallgrímskirkja church; ideal for first-time visitors who want to walk to everything.

A revitalized waterfront of old fish-processing warehouses turned into design studios, breweries, and the Maritime Museum; suits foodies and those catching whale-watching or Golden Circle tours nearby.
The main shopping street and its eastern end around the Hlemmur food hall, full of vintage shops, cafes and nightlife; great for younger travelers wanting energy after dark.
A leafy park district with Iceland's largest geothermal pool, a zoo and botanical garden; ideal for families and budget travelers using the campsite/hostel.
A quiet, residential seaside neighborhood near the university and domestic airport with a beloved local pool; suited to travelers wanting a local, low-key base a short walk from downtown.

water.note: Naturally pure spring-sourced tap water, safe to drink straight from the tap with no treatment needed.

transit.pay: Most riders pay via the Klapp app, which offers tap-to-pay virtual tickets and pre-paid trip bundles. Contactless bank cards can also be tapped on validators on many routes. Exact cash is accepted onboard but drivers give no change.
transit.hours: Most routes run roughly 6:30/7:00 AM to midnight on weekdays with reduced evening and Sunday frequency; there is no true late-night or 24-hour bus service.
transit.note: Reykjavík has no metro, tram, or train — Strætó buses are the only public transit system; the compact city center is very walkable, and renting a car is common for day trips outside town.

ferry: Viðey Island ferry (from Reykjavík Old Harbour)

transit.m: Flybus coach to BSÍ terminal (~45 min)
Strætó public bus route 55 (~1 hr, budget option)

tip.r: Service charge is included in restaurant and bar prices; tipping is not expected, though rounding up or a small tip for exceptional service is appreciated.

food.name: Pylsur
food.desc: Icelandic hot dog of lamb, pork and beef in a bun, ordered eina med ollu: ketchup, sweet mustard, remoulade, raw and crispy onions.

places.name: Baejarins Beztu Pylsur
places.note: A red cart since 1937 and the most famous food in Iceland; queue is part of it.

places.name: Pylsuvagninn Grensasvegi
places.note: The locals' hot dog stand away from downtown, open very late.

food.name: Plokkfiskur
food.desc: Mashed fish stew of poached cod or haddock with potato, onion and white sauce, served with dense dark rye bread and butter.

places.name: Islenski Barinn (The Icelandic Bar)
places.note: Menu built entirely around Icelandic staples; good place to try several at once.

places.name: Messinn
places.note: Fish restaurant known for pan-served seafood; consistently well reviewed.

places.name: Kaffivagninn
places.note: Harbour cafe since 1935, full of fishermen; the least touristy version in town.

food.name: Kjoetsupa
food.desc: Icelandic lamb soup with root vegetables, rice and herbs. Simple, salty and exactly what the weather calls for.

places.name: Cafe Loki
places.note: Opposite Hallgrimskirkja, serving traditional Icelandic plates including rye-bread ice cream.

places.name: Svarta Kaffid
places.note: Two soups a day served inside a hollowed-out sourdough loaf; a downtown fixture.

places.name: Islenski Barinn
places.note: Hearty bowl with rye bread, alongside a long Icelandic beer list.

food.name: Humarsupa (lobster soup)
food.desc: Creamy bisque made with Icelandic langoustine, richer and sweeter than it looks. Often eaten with a chunk of buttered bread.

places.name: Saegreifinn (Sea Baron)
places.note: Fishing-shack dining room famous for lobster soup and grilled fish skewers.

places.name: Messinn
places.note: Popular seafood kitchen; book ahead in summer as it fills quickly.

food.name: Icelandic lamb
food.desc: Free-roaming sheep graze on wild herbs all summer, giving the meat a clean, faintly gamey flavour. Best simply roasted or grilled.

places.name: Grillmarkadurinn
places.note: Wood-and-charcoal grill restaurant, showcase for Icelandic lamb and fish.

places.name: Thrir Frakkar
places.note: Small, long-established restaurant known for lamb and traditional seafood dishes.

places.name: Islenski Barinn
places.note: Casual lamb dishes for less money than the fine-dining rooms.

food.name: Skyr
food.desc: Thick, near fat-free cultured dairy, technically a cheese, eaten for a thousand years with cream and berries.

places.name: Cafe Loki
places.note: Traditional skyr with cream and brown sugar, on the Icelandic tasting plates.

places.name: Bakari Sandholt
places.note: Fifth-generation bakery doing skyr bowls, sourdough and excellent pastries.

places.name: Braud & Co
places.note: Bright-muralled bakery on the walk to Hallgrimskirkja; cinnamon rolls and skyr.

food.name: Brennivin
food.desc: Unsweetened caraway schnapps nicknamed Black Death, drunk ice-cold in a shot. Traditionally chased with fermented shark.

places.name: Islenski Barinn
places.note: Serves brennivin with hakarl for the full, brief, traditional experience.

places.name: Kaldi Bar
places.note: Relaxed bar from the Kaldi brewery with a solid happy hour and local spirits.

places.name: Lebowski Bar
places.note: Themed and touristy, but a fun late-night place to try local shots.

food.name: Icelandic craft beer
food.desc: Beer was banned in Iceland until 1989; the country has been catching up ever since with breweries like Kaldi, Borg and Einstok.

places.name: Skuli Craft Bar
places.note: Small bar near Austurvollur with the best rotating Icelandic tap list in town.

places.name: Kaldi Bar
places.note: Brewery-owned bar pouring the full Kaldi range; busy from happy hour onwards.

places.name: Bastard Brew & Food
places.note: Craft beer bar and kitchen just off Laugavegur; long Icelandic and imported tap list, open late.

landmarks: Hallgrímskirkja
Iceland's tallest church, its dramatic basalt-column-inspired concrete spire dominates the Reykjavík skyline and rewards climbers with sweeping views over the colorful city.
Harpa Concert Hall
A glittering glass concert hall on the waterfront, its honeycomb facade inspired by Iceland's basalt landscape shimmers with reflected light day and night.
Sun Voyager (Sólfar)
A sleek stainless-steel sculpture resembling a Viking ship skeleton on the shoreline, silhouetted dramatically against the sea and midnight sun.
Perlan
A futuristic glass-domed building perched atop geothermal hot water tanks, offering a rotating restaurant, planetarium, and one of the city's best viewpoints.
Reykjavík Old Harbour
A working fishing harbor turned lively waterfront district of colorful boats, seafood restaurants, and departure point for whale-watching tours into Faxaflói Bay.
Tjörnin (The Pond)
A tranquil downtown lake fringed by grassy banks and historic buildings, beloved for feeding resident ducks, swans, and Arctic terns in the heart of the city.
Alþingishúsið (Parliament House)
The dignified 19th-century seat of Iceland's Althing, one of the world's oldest parliaments, built from solid Icelandic dolerite in central Reykjavík.
Laugavegur
Reykjavík's main shopping street, lined with colorful facades, quirky boutiques, and buzzing cafes, and the traditional heart of the city's nightlife.
Grótta Lighthouse
A small white lighthouse on a tidal islet at the western tip of Reykjavík, a favorite spot for watching sunsets and hunting the northern lights.
Reykjavík Cathedral (Dómkirkjan)
A modest yet historic 18th-century cathedral beside the Parliament House, its simple white facade anchoring the old town's civic and religious core.

train.note: Iceland has no railways at all — no domestic or international trains. Long-distance travel around the island is by bus, rental car, or domestic flight.

bus.note: No international bus routes (Iceland is an island). Domestically, Strætó (straeto.is/en) runs the nationwide long-distance routes from Reykjavík, and Flybus and Airport Direct coaches link the city with Keflavík Airport.

ferry.note: Iceland's only international sea link, the Norröna car ferry, departs from Seyðisfjörður in east Iceland (~680 km from Reykjavík), not the capital. It sails weekly, mid-March to late November.

half.name: Þingvellir National Park
half.blurb: A rift valley between continental plates where Iceland's ancient parliament once met.

half.name: Gullfoss Waterfall
half.blurb: A thundering two-tiered waterfall plunging into a rugged glacial canyon.

half.name: Geysir Geothermal Area
half.blurb: Steaming hot springs where the Strokkur geyser erupts every few minutes.

half.name: Blue Lagoon
half.blurb: A milky-blue geothermal spa set amid a stark black lava field.

half.name: Reynisfjara Black Sand Beach
half.blurb: A dramatic volcanic beach with basalt columns and pounding Atlantic waves.

half.name: Seljalandsfoss Waterfall
half.blurb: A slender cascade you can walk behind for a fully enveloping view.
